definitions.text: The distal segment of the hind limb of vertebrates, including the tarsus and foot.
The motion of a horse when, raising his fore quarters, he keeps his hind feet on the ground without advancing; rearing.
A fee, or toll, paid for the weighing of merchandise.
See Pusane.
Made heavy or dull; debased. [Obs.] "Pesanted to each lewd thought's control." Marston.
See Peshito.
A pea. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A Spanish silver coin, and money of account, equal to about nineteen cents, and divided into 100 centesimos.
The earliest Syriac version of the Old Testament, translated from Hebrew; also, the incomplete Syriac version of the New Testament. [Written also peschito.]
The earliest Syriac version of the Old Testament, translated from Hebrew; also, the incomplete Syriac version of the New Testament. [Written also peschito.]
Pestering; vexatious; troublesome. Used also as an intensive. [Colloq. & Low, U.S.] Judd.
A Spanish dollar; also, an Argentine, Chilian, Colombian, etc., coin, equal to from 75 cents to a dollar; also, a pound weight.
(Metaph.)
The opinion or doctrine that everything in nature is ordered for or tends to the worst, or that the world is wholly evil; -- opposed to Ant: optimism.
A disposition to take the least hopeful view of things.
(Metaph.)
One who advocates the doctrine of pessimism; -- opposed to Ant: optimist.
One who looks on the dark side of things.
Of or pertaining to pessimism; characterized by pessimism; gloomy; foreboding. "Giving utterance to pessimistic doubt." Encyc. Brit.
Of or pertaining to pessimism; characterized by pessimism; gloomy; foreboding. "Giving utterance to pessimistic doubt." Encyc. Brit.
Pessimistic.
To hold or advocate the doctrine of pessimism. London Sat. Rev.
A delicate bar of cartilage connecting the dorsal and ventral extremities of the first pair of bronchial cartilages in the syrinx of birds.
A fatal epidemic disease; a pestilence; specif., the plague. England's sufferings by that scourge, the pest. Cowper.
Anything which resembles a pest; one who, or that which, is troublesome, noxious, mischievous, or destructive; a nuisance. "A pest and public enemy." South.

Belonging to, or characteristic of, a system of elementary education which combined manual training with other instruction, advocated and practiced by Jean Henri Pestalozzi (1746-1827), a Swiss teacher.
An advocate or follower of the system of Pestalozzi.
The system of education introduced by Pestalozzi.
To trouble; to disturb; to annoy; to harass with petty vexations. We are pestered with mice and rats. Dr. H. More. A multitude of scribblers daily pester the world. Dryden.
To crowd together in an annoying way; to overcrowd; to infest. All rivers and pools . . . pestered full with fishes. Holland.
One who pesters or harasses.
The act of pestering, or the state of being pestered; vexation; worry. "The trouble and pesterment of children." B. Franklin.
Inclined to pester. Also, vexatious; encumbering; burdensome.
Pestiferous. "After long and pestful calms." Coleridge.
A house or hospital for persons who are infected with any pestilential disease.
That which conveys contagion or infection. [Obs.] Donne.

Pest-bearing; pestilential; noxious to health; malignant; infectious; contagious; as, pestiferous bodies. "Poor, pestiferous creatures begging alms." Evelyn. "Unwholesome and pestiferous occupations." Burke.
Noxious to peace, to morals, or to society; vicious; hurtful; destructive; as, a pestiferous demagogue. Pestiferous reports of men very nobly held. Shak.
In a pestiferuos manner.
Specifically, the disease known as the plague; hence, any contagious or infectious epidemic disease that is virulent and devastating. The pestilence That walketh in darkness. Ps. xci. 6.

Fig.: That which is pestilent, noxious, or pernicious to the moral character of great numbers. I'll pour this pestilence into his ear. Shak. Pestilence weed (Bot.), the butterbur coltsfoot (Petasites vulgaris), so called because formerly considered a remedy for the plague. Dr. Prior.
Pestilential; noxious; pernicious; mischievous. "Corrupt and pestilent." Milton. "What a pestilent knave is this same!" Shak.
Having the nature or qualities of a pestilence. "Sends the pestilential vapors." Longfellow.
Hence: Mischievous; noxious; pernicious; morally destructive. So pestilential, so infectious a thing is sin. Jer. Taylor.
Pestilently.
Pestilential. [Obs.]
In a pestilent manner; mischievously; destructively. "Above all measure pestilently noisome." Dr. H. More.
The quality of being pestilent.
The act of pounding and bruising with a pestle in a mortar. Sir T. Browne.
An implement for pounding and breaking or braying substances in a mortar.
A constable's or bailiff's staff; -- so called from its shape.
The leg and leg bone of an animal, especially of a pig; as, a pestle of pork.
To pound, pulverize, bray, or mix with a pestle, or as with a pestle; to use a pestle.
